title: General Chemistry Practical II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L second-semester chemistry laboratory curriculum, building on CHM103: qualitative anion analysis, redox and gravimetric quantitative analysis, and basic organic separation/purification techniques (recrystallization, melting point determination, simple distillation, extraction).

questions.question: Addition of dilute hydrochloric acid to a solid sample, producing effervescence with a colourless gas that turns limewater milky, confirms the presence of which anion?
options: Chloride (Cl-)
Carbonate (CO3²-)
Sulphate (SO4²-)
Nitrate (NO3-)
questions.correct_answer: Carbonate (CO3²-)
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acids to release CO2 gas, which turns limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) milky due to formation of insoluble calcium carbonate.

questions.question: Acidified barium chloride solution added to a solution containing sulphate ions produces a:
options: Yellow precipitate soluble in acid
White precipitate (BaSO4) insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid
Blue precipitate
No visible reaction
questions.correct_answer: White precipitate (BaSO4) insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Barium sulphate is a white precipitate that is insoluble even in dilute acids, distinguishing sulphate from carbonate or sulphite, which dissolve in acid with effervescence.

questions.question: Silver nitrate solution is added to a solution containing chloride ions (in the presence of dilute nitric acid). The result observed is a:
options: Pale yellow precipitate soluble in concentrated ammonia only
White precipitate (AgCl), readily soluble in dilute ammonia solution
Cream precipitate insoluble in ammonia
No precipitate forms
questions.correct_answer: White precipitate (AgCl), readily soluble in dilute ammonia solution
questions.explanation: Silver chloride forms a white curdy precipitate that dissolves in dilute ammonia (forming a soluble diammine silver complex), distinguishing it from AgBr (cream, dissolves only in concentrated ammonia) and AgI (yellow, insoluble in ammonia).

questions.question: The 'brown ring test' is a confirmatory test used to identify the presence of which anion?
options: Sulphate
Nitrate
Chloride
Phosphate
questions.correct_answer: Nitrate
questions.explanation: In the brown ring test, freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate solution and concentrated sulphuric acid are added carefully to a nitrate solution; a brown ring forms at the interface due to a nitroso-iron(II) complex, confirming nitrate.

questions.question: Addition of dilute acid to a sample containing sulphite ions (SO3²-) typically releases a gas that:
options: Is odourless and relights a glowing splint
Has a pungent, choking smell (sulphur dioxide) and turns acidified potassium dichromate paper green
Is colourless, odourless, and does not react with any test paper
Turns damp red litmus paper blue
questions.correct_answer: Has a pungent, choking smell (sulphur dioxide) and turns acidified potassium dichromate paper green
questions.explanation: Sulphites release SO2 gas on acidification, which has a characteristic pungent odour and reduces orange acidified potassium dichromate paper to green (Cr³⁺).

questions.question: In qualitative anion analysis, a preliminary test in which a solid sample is heated alone (dry heating) can help identify anions such as carbonate by observing:
options: Formation of a permanent colourless liquid only
Evolution of gas, colour change, or sublimation characteristic of certain anions
No change is ever observed regardless of anion present
The sample becomes radioactive
questions.correct_answer: Evolution of gas, colour change, or sublimation characteristic of certain anions
questions.explanation: Dry heating tests are preliminary qualitative tests where observations like gas evolution, colour change, or sublimation give initial clues to the anions present before confirmatory wet tests.

questions.question: Lead(II) nitrate solution added to a solution suspected of containing iodide ions gives a characteristic:
options: White precipitate
Bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide
Blue solution
Brown gas
questions.correct_answer: Bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide
questions.explanation: Lead(II) iodide (PbI2) is a distinctive bright yellow precipitate, commonly used as a confirmatory test for iodide ions.

questions.question: In a redox titration between acidified potassium permanganate (KMnO4) and iron(II) sulphate, the end point is signalled by:
options: A colour change from purple to colourless as KMnO4 is added
The first permanent faint pink colour persisting in the solution, as KMnO4 acts as its own indicator
A green precipitate forming suddenly
The solution turning permanently blue
questions.correct_answer: The first permanent faint pink colour persisting in the solution, as KMnO4 acts as its own indicator
questions.explanation: KMnO4 is intensely coloured (purple) and is decolourized as it oxidizes Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺; once all Fe²⁺ is consumed, the next drop of KMnO4 gives a persistent faint pink colour, marking the end point.

questions.question: In permanganate titrations, the solution being titrated is typically acidified with dilute sulphuric acid rather than hydrochloric acid because:
options: Hydrochloric acid has no effect on the reaction
Chloride ions can be oxidized by KMnO4, introducing error into the titration
Sulphuric acid is a stronger acid than hydrochloric acid in all respects
Hydrochloric acid reacts explosively with KMnO4
questions.correct_answer: Chloride ions can be oxidized by KMnO4, introducing error into the titration
questions.explanation: KMnO4 can oxidize chloride ions to chlorine gas, consuming extra permanganate and giving an inaccurate (high) titre; dilute H2SO4 does not interfere in this way.

questions.question: In iodometric titrations, sodium thiosulphate solution is used to titrate liberated iodine, using which indicator near the end point?
options: Phenolphthalein
Starch indicator, which forms a deep blue-black colour with iodine
Methyl orange
Universal indicator
questions.correct_answer: Starch indicator, which forms a deep blue-black colour with iodine
questions.explanation: Starch forms an intense blue-black complex with iodine; it is added near the end point (when the solution is pale straw yellow) and the disappearance of the blue-black colour signals the end point.

questions.question: Complexometric titrations, such as the determination of water hardness (Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺), commonly use which titrant?
options: Potassium permanganate
EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid)
Sodium hydroxide
Silver nitrate
questions.correct_answer: EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid)
questions.explanation: EDTA forms stable 1:1 complexes with metal ions such as Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, making it the standard titrant for complexometric determination of water hardness.

questions.question: Eriochrome Black T is commonly used as an indicator in complexometric (EDTA) titrations because it:
options: Changes colour based on pH only, unrelated to metal ions
Forms a coloured complex with metal ions that is a different colour from the free indicator, signalling the end point when EDTA displaces the metal
Is used only to detect the presence of anions
Cannot be used in aqueous solution
questions.correct_answer: Forms a coloured complex with metal ions that is a different colour from the free indicator, signalling the end point when EDTA displaces the metal
questions.explanation: Eriochrome Black T forms a wine-red complex with metal ions like Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺; as EDTA is added and complexes all the free metal ions, the indicator is released in its free (blue) form at the end point.

questions.question: Gravimetric analysis determines the amount of an analyte in a sample by:
options: Measuring the volume of titrant consumed in a reaction
Precipitating, filtering, drying, and accurately weighing the analyte (or a compound derived from it)
Measuring the colour intensity of the solution
Timing how long a reaction takes to complete
questions.correct_answer: Precipitating, filtering, drying, and accurately weighing the analyte (or a compound derived from it)
questions.explanation: Gravimetric analysis is a quantitative method based on converting the analyte into a pure, insoluble compound of known composition, then isolating and weighing it precisely.

questions.question: In gravimetric analysis, a good precipitate for weighing should ideally be:
options: Highly soluble in the mother liquor to ease filtration
Of low purity but very large particle size
Insoluble, easily filterable, and of known, stable composition after drying/ignition
Coloured intensely so it can be seen easily, regardless of composition
questions.correct_answer: Insoluble, easily filterable, and of known, stable composition after drying/ignition
questions.explanation: A suitable gravimetric precipitate must be essentially insoluble (to minimize loss), easily separated from solution, pure, and convertible to a stable, well-defined compound for accurate weighing.

questions.question: Washing a precipitate during gravimetric analysis is done primarily to:
options: Increase the mass of the precipitate
Remove soluble impurities adhering to the precipitate without dissolving the precipitate itself
Dissolve the precipitate completely for re-analysis
Change the colour of the precipitate
questions.correct_answer: Remove soluble impurities adhering to the precipitate without dissolving the precipitate itself
questions.explanation: Washing (often with a dilute electrolyte solution or hot water) removes soluble contaminants from the precipitate surface while minimizing solubility losses of the precipitate.

questions.question: Recrystallization is a technique primarily used to:
options: Determine the melting point of a compound
Purify a solid organic compound by exploiting differences in solubility at different temperatures
Separate two miscible liquids
Measure the density of a liquid
questions.correct_answer: Purify a solid organic compound by exploiting differences in solubility at different temperatures
questions.explanation: Recrystallization purifies a solid by dissolving it in a hot solvent in which it is more soluble hot than cold, then cooling so the pure compound crystallizes out while impurities remain dissolved.

questions.question: A suitable solvent for recrystallizing a given compound should ideally:
options: Dissolve the compound well when cold, and poorly when hot
Dissolve the compound poorly when cold, and readily when hot, with impurities remaining soluble or easily removed
Dissolve neither the compound nor its impurities at any temperature
React chemically with the compound being purified
questions.correct_answer: Dissolve the compound poorly when cold, and readily when hot, with impurities remaining soluble or easily removed
questions.explanation: An ideal recrystallization solvent has high solubility for the compound at high temperature and low solubility at low temperature, allowing crystals to form on cooling while leaving impurities in solution.

questions.question: After recrystallization, the purified crystals are typically separated from the remaining solvent (mother liquor) by:
options: Evaporation to dryness of the entire mixture
Filtration (often suction/vacuum filtration)
Distillation of the crystals
Titration
questions.correct_answer: Filtration (often suction/vacuum filtration)
questions.explanation: Vacuum (Buchner) filtration efficiently separates the solid crystals from the mother liquor, and is faster and more thorough than gravity filtration for this purpose.

questions.question: Melting point determination is a useful technique in organic chemistry practicals mainly because:
options: It has no relation to the purity of a compound
A sharp melting point close to the literature value indicates a pure compound, while a broad or depressed range suggests impurity
It can only be used to identify inorganic salts
It measures the boiling point of a compound instead
questions.correct_answer: A sharp melting point close to the literature value indicates a pure compound, while a broad or depressed range suggests impurity
questions.explanation: Impurities typically lower and broaden the melting point range of a solid, so a sharp melting point matching the known literature value is used as a simple purity check.

questions.question: Simple distillation is most appropriate for separating:
options: Two miscible liquids with very close boiling points
A liquid from dissolved non-volatile solids, or two liquids with a large difference in boiling points
Two immiscible liquids of similar density
A mixture of two solids
questions.correct_answer: A liquid from dissolved non-volatile solids, or two liquids with a large difference in boiling points
questions.explanation: Simple distillation works well when separating a volatile liquid from non-volatile dissolved solids, or liquids whose boiling points differ substantially (usually by more than ~25°C).

questions.question: In a simple distillation setup, the thermometer bulb should be positioned:
options: Deep in the liquid being heated
Level with the side arm outlet of the distillation flask, to measure the temperature of the vapour passing into the condenser
Outside the apparatus entirely
At the very bottom of the condenser
questions.correct_answer: Level with the side arm outlet of the distillation flask, to measure the temperature of the vapour passing into the condenser
questions.explanation: Positioning the thermometer bulb at the side arm ensures it measures the temperature of the vapour actually leaving the flask and being condensed, which corresponds to the boiling point of the distillate.

questions.question: Liquid-liquid extraction using a separating funnel relies on the principle that:
options: All liquids are miscible and will mix into one layer
A solute distributes itself between two immiscible solvents according to its relative solubility in each
Only solids can be separated using a separating funnel
Extraction always requires heating to boiling
questions.correct_answer: A solute distributes itself between two immiscible solvents according to its relative solubility in each
questions.explanation: Liquid-liquid extraction exploits the differing solubility (partition) of a solute between two immiscible solvents, allowing it to be selectively transferred from one layer to the other.

questions.question: When using a separating funnel for extraction, after shaking and allowing the layers to settle, the tap is opened carefully with the funnel inverted mainly to:
options: Speed up evaporation of the solvent
Release built-up pressure from volatile solvents and prevent the stopper from being forced out
Mix the two layers further
Cool the contents of the funnel
questions.correct_answer: Release built-up pressure from volatile solvents and prevent the stopper from being forced out
questions.explanation: Shaking with volatile solvents builds internal pressure; venting periodically by opening the tap with the funnel inverted prevents dangerous pressure build-up.

questions.question: In an EDTA titration to determine the total hardness of a water sample, 20.0 cm³ of water sample required 15.0 cm³ of 0.01 mol/dm³ EDTA to reach the end point. The number of moles of Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺ (assuming 1:1 stoichiometry with EDTA) in the titre volume is:
options: 0.15 mol
questions.explanation: Moles of EDTA = moles of metal ion (1:1) = 0.01 mol/dm³ × 0.015 dm³ = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol.

questions.question: A student obtains a gravimetric precipitate of BaSO4 with a mass of 0.466 g from a sample. If the molar mass of BaSO4 is 233 g/mol, the number of moles of sulphate originally present is:
options: 0.02 mol
0.2 mol
2.0 mol
questions.explanation: Moles of BaSO4 = mass/molar mass = 0.466/233 = 0.002 mol, which equals the moles of sulphate ion originally present (1:1 stoichiometry).

questions.question: In a redox titration, 25.0 cm³ of an acidified Fe²⁺ solution required 20.0 cm³ of 0.02 mol/dm³ KMnO4 for complete oxidation. Given the ionic equation MnO4⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O, the concentration of Fe²⁺ in the original solution is:
options: 0.016 mol/dm³
0.08 mol/dm³
0.004 mol/dm³
0.16 mol/dm³
questions.correct_answer: 0.08 mol/dm³
questions.explanation: Moles KMnO4 = 0.02 × 0.020 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol; moles Fe²⁺ = 5 × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol; concentration = 2.0 × 10⁻³/0.025 = 0.08 mol/dm³.

questions.question: Percentage yield in a practical preparation is calculated as:
options: (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) × 100%
(Theoretical yield / Actual yield) × 100%
Actual yield − Theoretical yield
Actual yield + Theoretical yield
questions.correct_answer: (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) × 100%
questions.explanation: Percentage yield compares the actual (experimentally obtained) mass of product to the theoretical (maximum possible) mass calculated from stoichiometry, expressed as a percentage.

questions.question: A laboratory report on a quantitative practical should always include an estimate of experimental error because:
options: It is required only for organic experiments
It allows evaluation of the reliability of the result and identification of possible sources of inaccuracy
It has no real scientific value
It replaces the need to record any observations
questions.correct_answer: It allows evaluation of the reliability of the result and identification of possible sources of inaccuracy
questions.explanation: Reporting error/uncertainty allows the reader to judge how reliable the result is and helps the experimenter identify and account for sources of systematic or random error.

questions.question: Sublimation is a useful purification technique for a solid compound when that compound:
options: Decomposes well below its melting point
Can pass directly from the solid to the gaseous state (and back) without melting, while impurities do not
Is highly soluble in every common solvent
Is a liquid at room temperature
questions.correct_answer: Can pass directly from the solid to the gaseous state (and back) without melting, while impurities do not
questions.explanation: Sublimation purifies solids that vaporize directly without melting (e.g., iodine, naphthalene); the vapour is then re-deposited as a pure solid on a cool surface, leaving non-subliming impurities behind.

questions.question: Steam distillation is particularly useful for isolating:
options: Water-soluble salts from aqueous solution
Volatile, water-immiscible organic compounds from a mixture containing non-volatile material, at a temperature below 100°C
Two miscible liquids of identical boiling point
Non-volatile solids only
questions.correct_answer: Volatile, water-immiscible organic compounds from a mixture containing non-volatile material, at a temperature below 100°C
questions.explanation: Steam distillation allows a water-immiscible volatile compound to co-distil with steam at a temperature below the boiling point of water, protecting heat-sensitive compounds and separating them from non-volatile residues.

questions.question: Activated charcoal (decolourizing carbon) is sometimes added during recrystallization to:
options: Increase the mass of the final crystals
Adsorb coloured impurities from the hot solution before filtration
Lower the melting point of the product deliberately
React chemically with the desired product
questions.correct_answer: Adsorb coloured impurities from the hot solution before filtration
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal has a large adsorptive surface area that removes coloured (and some other) impurities from a hot solution; it is removed by hot filtration before the solution is cooled to crystallize.

questions.question: After filtration, purified crystals are often stored in a desiccator before weighing or melting point determination in order to:
options: Add moisture to the crystals
Keep the crystals dry by preventing reabsorption of atmospheric moisture
Heat the crystals gently
Dissolve any remaining impurities
questions.correct_answer: Keep the crystals dry by preventing reabsorption of atmospheric moisture
questions.explanation: A desiccator contains a drying agent that maintains a low-humidity environment, preventing purified, dried crystals from reabsorbing moisture before they are weighed or analysed.
